orders.description: Defendant’s appeal from the September 10, 2009 denial of summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell in defendant’s store but could not identify why. She attributed the fall to ice cream an employee noticed a few feet away about 20 minutes later; there were no skid or track marks there and no evidence of how long the ice cream had been present.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant demonstrated plaintiff could not identify the cause. Linking the fall to ice cream observed later and nearby, without skid marks or duration evidence, would be speculative; plaintiff raised no triable issue.

quality.notes: The actual store interior supports private retail control, but title/lease role, plaintiff’s role and accident date are unstated. Hazard remains unclear: ice cream was observed after the accident and is only a speculative causal explanation. Twenty minutes is the post-fall observation delay, not a proven pre-fall hazard duration. The opinion does not identify a deposition, affidavit, photograph or other evidence format; an employee observation alone does not establish witness-testimony format. Duration is discussed for causation, not as a separate constructive-notice holding. Reversal grants dismissal and favors defendant.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.

The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell in the defendant’s store. She could not identify the reason for her fall, but concluded that she slipped on ice cream that an employee noticed on the floor a few feet away approximately 20 minutes after the accident. There were no skid or track marks where the ice cream was located and no evidence as to how long it had been on the floor.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendant appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Markey, J.), dated September 10, 2009, which denied its motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Here, the defendant established its prima facie entitlement to summary judgment by demonstrating that the plaintiff could not identify the cause of her fall

Given that inability, and the lack of any skid marks where the ice cream was located or evidence as to how long it had been there, any conclusion that the ice cream caused the plaintiff to fall would be based entirely on speculation
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact
Consequently, the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint should have been granted.
We reverse.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the January 31, 2018 denial of dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on snow on the marble tile floor of the vestibule of defendants’ Brooklyn supermarket at about 7:00 p.m. on February 21, 2015.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants were not required to cover every floor with mats or continuously mop tracked-in precipitation. Liability could still arise from creation or notice with reasonable time to remedy; defendants established the applicable noncreation/notice showing.
Defendants established noncreation of the alleged vestibule condition prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The opinion does not detail the underlying proof.
Defendants established lack of actual notice prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The opinion does not detail the underlying proof.

Defendants established lack of constructive notice for sufficient time to discover and remedy the condition prima facie, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The opinion does not detail the underlying proof.

quality.notes: The actual supermarket vestibule supports private retail control and is coded entrance. The opinion does not expressly identify ownership/lease roles, plaintiff customer status or evidence formats. Snow is the alleged condition; water/ice in the general rule is not added as a case fact. Tracked-in precipitation analysis is not a storm-in-progress holding and does not establish whether precipitation was occurring at the accident time. No continuous-mopping requirement does not eliminate all reasonable-care obligations. The full reversal grants dismissal and favors defendants.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is reversed, on the law, with costs, and the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint is granted.
On February 21, 2015, at about 7:00 p.m., the plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell on snow on the marble tile floor of the vestibule of the defendants' supermarket in Brooklyn.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Devin P. Cohen, J.), dated January 31, 2018. The order denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
While a defendant is not required to cover all of its floors with mats, or to continuously mop up all moisture resulting from tracked-in precipitation

a defendant may be held liable for an injury proximately caused by a dangerous condition created by water, snow, or ice tracked into a building if it either created the hazardous condition, or had actual or constructive notice of the condition and a reasonable time to undertake remedial action

Here, the defendants established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that they did not create the alleged hazardous condition in the vestibule or have actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to have discovered and remedied it
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiffs’ appeal from the February 24, 2012 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Elizabeth Boyle allegedly tripped over a cardboard box in an aisle of defendant’s store. The opinion does not describe the box’s dimensions or who placed it there.

legal_issues.finding: Defendant established prima facie that the box condition was readily observable and not inherently dangerous as a matter of law. Plaintiffs’ expert affidavit did not raise a triable issue; visibility alone is not the whole holding.
Plaintiffs’ professional engineer affidavit was speculative, conclusory and without foundation, and failed to raise a triable issue. The opinion does not reproduce its theory or measurements.

evidence_discussed.description: Plaintiffs submitted a professional engineer’s affidavit in opposition, found speculative, conclusory and lacking foundation.

quality.notes: Private store ownership and trip over a box are express. Injured role and accident date are unstated. The holding combines open-and-obvious with absence of inherent danger; it does not announce that every visible obstruction is safe. No creation/notice ruling, trivial-defect determination or code-violation theory is inferred. Expert shortcomings are stated but the opinion does not identify an oath/admissibility defect, inspection details or quantitative measurements.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff Elizabeth Boyle allegedly was injured when she tripped and fell over a cardboard box in the aisle of a store owned by the defendant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, etc., the plaintiffs appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Mayer, J), dated February 24, 2012, which granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

On its motion for summary judgment, the defendant made a prima facie showing that the complained-of condition was both open and obvious, i.e., readily observable by those employing the reasonable use of their senses, and not inherently dangerous as a matter of law
In opposition, while the plaintiffs submitted the affidavit of a professional engineer, the affidavit was speculative, conclusory, and lacking in foundation
and thus failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the February 23, 2018 order dismissing claims against Enid Russillo.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted Enid Russillo’s motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff, a police officer responding to an emergency call at Enid Russillo’s home, allegedly slipped on a wet single-step riser on the morning of January 29, 2014. The source of the wetness is not identified.

legal_issues.finding: On common-law negligence, defendant established noncreation of the alleged step condition prima facie, with the ongoing emergency part of the context, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The statutory claim has a different notice standard and failed for lack of requisite culpability.

On common-law negligence, defendant established lack of actual notice prima facie, with the ongoing emergency part of the context, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The statutory claim has a different notice standard and failed for lack of requisite culpability.

On common-law negligence, defendant established lack of constructive notice for sufficient time to discover and remedy the condition prima facie, with the ongoing emergency part of the context, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The statutory claim has a different notice standard and failed for lack of requisite culpability.

The GML § 205-e claim required an identified legal predicate and culpable noncompliance. Defendant established lack of requisite culpability for the alleged violations, and plaintiff raised no triable issue. The particular predicate provisions are not identified in this opinion.

General Municipal Law § 205-e supplies a police-officer statutory cause of action distinct from common-law negligence. Ordinary actual/constructive notice of the particular defect is unnecessary, but neglect, omission or willful/culpable negligence must underlie the violation; defendant established that culpability was lacking.

quality.notes: An officer’s emergency response does not convert the explicitly owned home into public property or make this a Labor Law case. Injured role other denotes responding police officer; defendant is owner. Wet step is other because the wetting substance is unspecified. Medical detail beyond the existence of an emergency is omitted from the factual summary. The statutory lack-of-culpability holding is not a ruling that ordinary notice is required under GML § 205-e or a finding that no predicate violation existed. No firefighter-rule/assumption-of-risk defense or particular building-code provision is inferred. One appealed order, fully affirmed as to the appealed defendant, is label 0. Evidence formats are not identified. Preliminary validation-period case: unchanged initial rules applied without tuning.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.

On the morning of January 29, 2014, the plaintiff, a Nassau County police officer, allegedly was injured when he slipped and fell on a wet single-step riser located at premises owned by the defendant Enid Russillo (hereinafter the defendant).

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (John H. Rouse, J.), dated February 23, 2018. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted the motion of the defendant Enid Russillo for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her.
The plaintiff was at the defendant's home in connection with an emergency call involving the defendant's mother, who had been found unresponsive and not breathing.
The plaintiff subsequently commenced this personal injury action against, among others, the defendant, alleging common-law negligence and a violation of General Municipal Law § 205-e.

Here, the defendant established her prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that she did not create the allegedly hazardous condition on the step, or have actual or constructive notice of its existence for a sufficient length of time to have discovered and remedied it, particularly given the ongoing emergency involving her mother
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact

To establish a cause of action under General Municipal Law § 205-e, a police officer plaintiff must (1) identify the statute or ordinance with which the defendant allegedly failed to comply, (2) describe the manner in which the police officer was injured, and (3) set forth facts from which it may be inferred that the defendant's negligence directly or indirectly caused the harm

Although recovery under General Municipal Law § 205-e does not require proof of such notice as would be necessary to a common-law negligence cause of action, i.e., actual or constructive notice of the particular defect on the premises causing injury, the plaintiff still must establish that the circumstances surrounding the violation indicate that it was a result of neglect, omission, or willful or culpable negligence on the defendant's part
Here, the defendant established, prima facie, that "the requisite culpability for the [alleged] violation[s] [was] lacking"
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted the defendant's motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her.

orders.description: Defendants’ appeal from the February 1, 2016 denial of summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Denied defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped while descending exterior steps in front of defendants’ house. She alleged defendants painted the steps with paint unsuitable for exterior stairs; defendants contended they maintained the premises safely.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants contended they maintained the premises reasonably safely. The court did not separately define the general maintenance duty; it held their showing failed to address the specific code allegations.

Plaintiff alleged defendants created an unsafe condition by applying unsuitable paint. The court resolved the failure to address the code allegations without separately deciding whether negligent painting created a hazard.

Defendants failed to address the specific Administrative Code §§ 27-375 and 27-376 allegations and thus failed to establish compliance or inapplicability prima facie. The court did not find either provision applicable or violated; opposition sufficiency was immaterial.

quality.notes: The residence’s exterior steps, defendants’ asserted maintenance and the specific allegation of their painting support private residential control; title/lease roles remain unstated. This is a staircase of the house rather than a generically described adjacent sidewalk. Paint is other, not a confirmed structural stair defect or known chemical. Injured role and accident date are unknown. Failure to establish compliance/inapplicability is not an adjudicated code violation. No expert or documentary evidence format, notice finding or procedural-only issue is inferred. The appealed denial is fully affirmed and favors plaintiff at this stage, without establishing liability.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell while walking down a set of exterior steps in front of the defendants' house.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the defendants appeal from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Schack, J.), dated February 1, 2016, which denied their motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The plaintiff alleges that the defendants negligently painted the steps with a type of paint that was not intended for use on exterior stairs in violation of sections 27-375 and 27-376 of the Administrative Code of the City of New York.
After discovery had been completed, the defendants moved for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, contending that they maintained the premises in a reasonably safe condition.

The defendants did not address the plaintiff's specific allegations that the exterior steps violated Administrative Code §§ 27-375 and 27-376, and thus failed to establish, prima facie, either that the steps were in compliance with those sections, or that those sections were inapplicable
Since the defendants failed to meet their initial burden as the movants, it is not necessary to review the sufficiency of the plaintiff's opposition papers
